## Reduce backend latency

Reduce the time between a request for backend work and a useful result for the conversation. Measure [latency at each stage](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/voice-agents#measure-latency) to locate delays. Compare useful spoken response time and task success on the same scenarios, and see the [voice agent evaluation Cookbook](https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/audio/voice_agent_evaluation) for evaluation guidance.



  


### Responses delegation

Live manages persistent WebSocket connections to Responses and prepares known request configuration in advance. It can also reuse prior response state when the active connection and state support it. Measure response time and reported cache usage on your workload to see the effect.

Tune the backend through `delegation.responses`:

- `model`: choose the model that handles reasoning and tool selection independently of the voice model.
- `reasoning.effort`: balance reasoning time and task quality using values supported by that model.
- `service_tier`: use `auto`, `default`, `flex`, or `priority`, subject to model support and project access. `auto` follows the project's configuration. Evaluate the performance and cost of the tier you choose.

Update supported settings during the session with `session.update`. Your custom tools still run in your application, so slow service calls, queues, and tool-result buffering can delay the answer even when Live manages the Responses connection. Return each required tool result promptly and [continue the backend response](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-delegation?delegation-mode=responses#complete-a-client-actionable-function-call).

  

  


### Client delegation

Your application owns the path from delegation receipt to returning a result. Prepare that path while the voice session runs:

- **Reuse backend connections.** Keep the API client and its connection pool alive across delegations. For repeated Responses calls, consider a persistent [Responses WebSocket](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/websocket-mode).
- **Prepare known configuration.** Initialize instructions, tools, and connections before the first request needs them. Responses WebSocket mode also supports warming up known request state before generation; follow its [setup guidance](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/websocket-mode#connect-and-create-responses).
- **Stream useful results.** Return coherent, verified chunks with `session.commentary.append`. Use `session.thinking.append` for quiet progress. Preserve the client delegation ID and the 500-token limit per append. Keep private reasoning in the backend and confirm actions before announcing success.
- **Keep reusable input stable.** Preserve instructions, tool definitions and ordering, and unchanged history prefixes. Append new information after reusable content when your backend supports caching and continuation.
- **Forward complete, useful updates.** Send each result as soon as you have enough text to understand it on its own. Have your backend label updates as progress or results so your application can choose the appropriate append event. If it marks these categories with a text prefix, wait for the full prefix before forwarding the update.

Measure the first useful spoken answer when comparing this path with Responses delegation.

  




### React to transcript fragments

Processing transcript fragments in your application is optional and works with either delegation mode. User and assistant [transcript fragments](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-conversations#transcript-deltas) arrive over WebSocket or the WebRTC data channel. You can process them with application logic or a lightweight model to start work before a delegation event arrives, or use the transcript itself to trigger application-owned work.

Use this pattern to:

- **Reduce waiting.** Start a speculative lookup when enough information is available—for example, checking availability while the user continues describing their preferences.
- **Run guardrails.** Check the growing transcript for requests or responses that need intervention. See [Apply conversation guardrails](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/voice-server-controls?api=live#apply-conversation-guardrails).
- **Adapt the conversation.** Look for wording that suggests confusion or frustration, then adjust the experience or send a focused instruction.
- **Update the interface.** Highlight relevant controls, populate suggested fields, or show results as they become available.

For browser applications, use the WebRTC data channel for captions and local UI updates. When transcript processing runs on your server—for guardrails, lightweight model checks, or speculative tool calls—use a [sideband WebSocket](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/voice-server-controls?api=live#decide-whether-you-need-a-sideband) to receive events and steer the same GPT-Live session directly.

Process accumulated text when meaningful new information arrives. A fragment may be incomplete, and later speech can change the request. Discard outdated results, coordinate with subsequent delegated work to avoid duplicate actions, and apply your usual permission and confirmation checks before consequential actions.

Send findings or instructions back to GPT-Live using the [append event that matches the update](#send-the-right-kind-of-update). For work started outside a client delegation, use `delegation_id: null`. Your application applies UI changes and manages tool execution and cancellation.

### Shared optimizations

Both delegation modes benefit from the same backend improvements:

- **Choose the model and reasoning effort for the task.** Compare configurations that meet your accuracy requirements. Use lower reasoning effort when it completes the task reliably.
- **Keep answers concise.** Return the facts and status GPT-Live needs to continue the conversation. Avoid long explanations and extra model calls just to rewrite results for speech.
- **Reduce tool delays and unnecessary calls.** Start authorized work when its inputs are ready, reuse results while they remain valid, and avoid repeating a completed lookup.
- **Run independent work concurrently.** Independent lookup calls can run together. Respect dependencies and required confirmations for actions. `parallel_tool_calls` lets a model request multiple calls; your application still schedules and executes its custom functions.

See [Latency optimization](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/latency-optimization) for general Responses guidance and [Prompt caching](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching) for reusing stable input.

## Verify the complete interaction

Verify that the backend completed the intended action and that the client played the expected spoken result. For example, check both the booking record and the audio played after a successful reservation. The backend can finish while the spoken answer is interrupted, so test these outcomes separately.

Track each application action with its own operation ID and each changed request with a task revision, alongside the GPT-Live delegation ID. Use those records to recognize completed work after reconnects or retries and to discard results for outdated requests.

Use [Evaluating voice agents](https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/audio/voice_agent_evaluation) for repeatable tests. For an existing Realtime tool loop or chained backend, follow [Migrate to GPT-Live](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-migration).

## Steer the live conversation from your application

Responses delegation manages the backend workflow, but your application can still send context directly to the GPT-Live model. ## Handle Responses delegation

For Responses-backed work, `session.delegation.created` has `target: "responses"` and a `response_id`. Subsequent Responses events arrive inside a `response.event` envelope:

```json
{
  "type": "response.event",
  "event_id": "event_response_1",
  "delegation_id": "item_9tA2cB6n2V8c4X1z7Q5r9",
  "event": {
    "type": "response.output_text.delta",
    "sequence_number": 4,
    "item_id": "msg_123",
    "output_index": 0,
    "content_index": 0,
    "delta": "The forecast is",
    "logprobs": []
  }
}
```

When the top-level event type is `response.event`, dispatch on `envelope.event.type`. Save the outer `delegation_id` to associate the backend event with its delegation. Your handler may also receive nested Responses lifecycle events beyond those shown here.

Live speech and delegated work continue independently. A completed backend response does not itself mean the user heard the answer. Use the Live output transcript and audio for the spoken part of the interaction.





### Run a custom function and return its result

Track the response ID from nested `response.created` alongside the outer `delegation_id`. Collect the response's function calls from `response.output_item.done`, and use that collection to determine which tool results to submit before continuing.

The forwarded lifecycle events, including `response.completed`, contain `response.output: []` even when function calls need results. These events also have an empty `tools` array, `instructions: null`, and no `input` field. Read the individual output-item events for the function calls.

| System-level instructions for the live model, such as a greeting, disclosure, or direction to stop speaking | `session.instructions.append` |

import { mutationGeneric, type GenericMutationCtx } from "convex/server";
import { v } from "convex/values";
import { GRANT_CATALOG } from "@notorganic/core";
import { requireGatewaySecret } from "./lib";
import { issueGrantFunds } from "./wallet";
import type { DataModel } from "./_generated/dataModel";

export const KEATING_WELCOME_AMOUNT_MICROS = 2_500_000;
export const KEATING_WELCOME_PROGRAM = "keating_welcome";

export interface WelcomeCredit {
  eligible: boolean;
  // True after issuance, including when the one-time credit has been spent.
  granted: boolean;
  amountMicros: number;
  remainingMicros: number;
}

/** Caller must supply the DID and product established by authenticated gateway use. */
export async function ensureKeatingWelcomeGrant(
  ctx: GenericMutationCtx<DataModel>,
  input: { did: string; product: string },
): Promise<WelcomeCredit> {
  const unavailable: WelcomeCredit = {
    eligible: false, granted: false,
    amountMicros: KEATING_WELCOME_AMOUNT_MICROS, remainingMicros: 0,
  };
  if (input.product !== "keating") return unavailable;
  const idempotencyKey = `keating-welcome:${input.did}`;
  const existing = await ctx.db.query("grantLots")
    .withIndex("by_idempotency", q => q.eq("idempotencyKey", idempotencyKey)).unique();
  if (existing) {
    if (existing.did !== input.did || existing.program !== KEATING_WELCOME_PROGRAM ||
      existing.amountMicros !== KEATING_WELCOME_AMOUNT_MICROS || existing.productScope !== "keating" ||
      existing.expiresAt !== null) throw new Error("IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT");
    return { ...unavailable, granted: true, remainingMicros: existing.remainingMicros };
  }

  const account = await ctx.db.query("didAccounts")
    .withIndex("by_did", q => q.eq("did", input.did)).unique();
  if (account && (account.deletedAt !== undefined || account.recoveryState !== "active")) return unavailable;

  // Cash deposits and purchased/shared paid-plan grant lots are durable payment
  // history. Check history, not the current balance: spending or expiry must not
  // turn a previously funded account into a new free account.
  const deposit = await ctx.db.query("walletEntries")
    .withIndex("by_did_created", q => q.eq("did", input.did))
    .filter(q => q.and(q.eq(q.field("kind"), "deposit"), q.gt(q.field("amountMicros"), 0)))
    .first();
  if (deposit) return unavailable;
  const paidPrograms = Object.keys(GRANT_CATALOG).filter(program => program !== "interleave_free");
  const paidGrant = await ctx.db.query("grantLots")
    .withIndex("by_did_expiry", q => q.eq("did", input.did))
    .filter(q => q.or(...paidPrograms.map(program => q.eq(q.field("program"), program))))
    .first();
  if (paidGrant) return unavailable;

  // This read plus issueGrantFunds' idempotency read/write share one Convex
  // transaction, including retries under concurrent sign-ins and devices.
  const id = await issueGrantFunds(ctx, {
    did: input.did, program: KEATING_WELCOME_PROGRAM,
    amountMicros: KEATING_WELCOME_AMOUNT_MICROS,
    productScope: "keating", expiresAt: null, idempotencyKey,
    reason: "One-time Keating welcome credit for an account without purchased credits",
  }, "keating-welcome");
  const grant = await ctx.db.get("grantLots", id);
  return {
    eligible: true, granted: true, amountMicros: KEATING_WELCOME_AMOUNT_MICROS,
    remainingMicros: grant!.remainingMicros,
  };
}

export const ensure = mutationGeneric({
  args: { serviceSecret: v.string(), did: v.string(), product: v.string() },
  handler: async (ctx, args): Promise<WelcomeCredit> => {
    requireGatewaySecret(args.serviceSecret);
    return await ensureKeatingWelcomeGrant(ctx, args);
  },
});

name: playwriter
description: Control the user own Chrome browser via Playwriter extension with Playwright code snippets in a stateful local js sandbox via playwriter cli. Use this over other Playwright MCPs to automate the browser — it connects to the user's existing Chrome instead of launching a new one. Use this for JS-heavy websites (Instagram, Twitter, cookie/login walls, lazy-loaded UIs) instead of webfetch/curl. Run `playwriter skill` command to read the complete up to date skill
---

## REQUIRED: Read Full Documentation First

**Before using playwriter, you MUST run this command:**

```bash
playwriter skill # IMPORTANT! do not use | head here. read in full!
```

This outputs the complete documentation including:

- Session management and timeout configuration
- Selector strategies (and which ones to AVOID)
- Rules to prevent timeouts and failures
- Best practices for slow pages and SPAs
- Context variables, utility functions, and more

**Do NOT skip this step.** The quick examples below will fail without understanding timeouts, selector rules, and common pitfalls from the full docs.

**Read the ENTIRE output.** Do NOT pipe through `head`, `tail`, or any truncation command. The skill output must be read in its entirety — critical rules about timeouts, selectors, and common pitfalls are spread throughout the document, not just at the top.

## Minimal Example (after reading full docs)

```bash
playwriter session new
playwriter -s 1 -e 'await page.goto("https://example.com")'
```

**Always use single quotes** for the `-e` argument. Single quotes prevent bash from interpreting `$`, backticks, and backslashes inside your JS code. Use double quotes or backtick template literals for strings inside the JS.

If `playwriter` is not found, use `npx playwriter@latest` or `bunx playwriter@latest`.

# Live voice in Twyne

Character comments resolve their narrator before synthesis. The player shows cast names for OpenAI, Fish Audio, and browser voices; browser narration maps the cast to supported Supertonic embeddings. An explicit voice change affects the active passage, not the next character’s comment.

The voice desk opens from **Talk** in the compositor, a character note, or the narration player. It uses Not Organic’s existing `/v1/live/sessions` route with `gpt-live-1`. `/api/live` only bridges the browser’s WebSocket to the authenticated gateway; Twyne does not receive an OpenAI key. The gateway currently selects Marin for live audio, while the chosen editor supplies their role and speaking direction.

Live supports simultaneous microphone input and speech output, separate captions, mute, graceful end, and client delegation. Requests can find draft passages, search via the existing research provider, open editorial panels, and propose replacements or additions. Edits require a later spoken approval or the Apply button, check the document revision, preserve surrounding rich text, and participate in the editor’s undo history. Switching folios ends the conversation. Search refuses the research provider’s local placeholder results.

## Credit and access

Pro members and accounts with unspent Twyne welcome credit can start Live. The provider grants eligible accounts a one-time $2.50 Twyne allowance, using the same paid-history exclusions and transactional idempotency as the existing Keating allowance. The allowance is scoped to Twyne and cannot be replenished by signing in again.

Each voice session reserves up to $0.50. The gateway enforces duration from its configured rate and settles trusted final usage. Each delegated language request has a separate $0.05 maximum and uses the wallet-backed `fast` route. The UI discloses these separate limits; they are spending ceilings, not advertised model rates. Closing the microphone releases local capture immediately while the connection waits for `session.closed`. An unconfirmed final receipt is shown as such.

## Configuration and rollout

Both the Twyne server and Convex must use the same `NOTORGANIC_ISSUER` (default `https://api.notorganic.info`). Production must set `SITE_URL` to the public Twyne origin for the WebSocket origin check. Existing Not Organic assertion credentials remain server-side. The gateway must have GPT Live enabled, its rate configured, and the Twyne product authorized for `realtime:connect`, `wallet:read`, and `infer:fast`. Research uses Twyne’s existing research configuration.

The companion provider changes are in `convex/welcomeGrants.ts`, `apps/gateway/src/convex-store.ts`, and `apps/gateway/src/live.ts`. The Live policy accepts delegated replies only for IDs observed from the upstream session; it still rejects Responses delegation, arbitrary model changes, storage, and client-supplied usage. Deploy those provider changes and Twyne’s `convex/liveVoice.ts` before exposing the frontend.

Provider processing/content-logging consent is recorded by Not Organic. Twyne keeps captions only in session memory and does not save microphone recordings. Pending work is abandoned when the session closes; paid requests already dispatched may still settle.

Protocol references: [GPT Live sessions](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-conversations), [client delegation](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-delegation).

Deterministic checks cover character selection, credit eligibility, relay handshake restrictions, revision-safe edits, one-time grants, delegated reply IDs, and provider settlement after disconnect. A real microphone conversation, actual wallet debit, and production deployment must still be verified separately.

## Task 3: Four central questions for the hiring article

### rollout_summary_files

- rollout_summaries/REDACTED.md (cwd=/home/diogenes/Documents/Codex/2026-08-23/realtime-voice-chat, rollout_path=/home/diogenes/.codex/sessions/2026/08/23/rollout-2026-08-23T21-52-55-01a03178-7f5a-7483-8a85-9ab075402487.jsonl, updated_at=2026-08-29T07:46:17+00:00, thread_id=01a03178-7f5a-7483-8a85-9ab075402487, success; user approved four-question set)

### keywords

- Engineering levels aren’t about skill anymore, Swizec Teller, baseline coding bar, solution refinement, staff, tradeoffs, observable evidence, four questions

## User preferences

- when early growth planning, the user wants direct, person-by-person discovery: personally onboard likely builders/writers/learners/students, observe repeated use, record exact language and current behavior, then ask for introductions after a real result [Task 1]
- the user wants Mom Test-style conversations and two poster designs, not hypothetical “would you use this?” questions; product walkthrough videos should show real jobs and support onboarding as well as marketing [Task 1]
- payment is the shared launch gateway: web first, desktop first-class where practical, mobile deferred until production-ready; NotOrganic Provider must own browser authentication, checkout, webhooks, subscriptions, and entitlements [Task 2]
- the user wants exact status distinctions between local implementation, targeted verification, deployment, and real provider proof [Task 2]
- “remove em dashes” and use exactly four central questions when translating hiring claims into observable engineering work and evidence [Task 3]

## Reusable knowledge

- Stage attributable experiments: at $8 CPM, 1% CTR, and 2% visitor-to-paid conversion, $100 is a smoke test, $500 is directional, and $2,000 is larger but still noisy. Keep audience, product, landing page, posters, podcasts, and warm outreach separately attributable. At $12/month and three-month retention, gross revenue is $36, so early CAC should stay materially below that until margin and retention are proven. [Task 1]
- Campus/outdoor placement is permission-controlled. uOttawa external posting needs approval, bilingual French-first creative, stamped posters, and limited periods; Carleton's general policy excludes commercial promotion. Use approved venues or permission-based placements, a concrete use case, QR plus short URL, and per-venue tracking. [Task 1]
- NotOrganic Provider is the sole authority for identity, consent, checkout, webhooks, subscriptions, wallet/usage, and entitlements. A public Keating client needs strict redirect validation, S256 PKCE, narrow scopes, a public DPoP key, a short-lived one-time code, atomic verifier/binding validation before code consumption, and provider-state feature gates rather than local Pro flags. [Task 2]
- The approved hiring prompts ask about: baseline coding beyond an algorithm screen; recurring work separating junior through staff; observable evidence for solution refinement; and assessment of technical, economic, operational, and stakeholder judgment. [Task 3]

## Failures and how to do differently

- Treat QR engagement, poster scans, retention, and acquisition math as hypotheses, not forecasts. Do not enter residences, knock on private doors, or leave materials in private common areas; use consented brief public intercepts, approved tables/events, and 20–30 simple outcomes. [Task 1]
- Never consume an authorization code before PKCE/verifier and binding checks: a prior implementation let an invalid verifier burn a valid code. No deployment, charge, provider-delivered webhook, entitlement update, or authenticated portal session was proven; local passes are not a production-complete payment funnel. [Task 2]

3223	## User preferences
  3224	
  3225	- when early growth planning, the user wants direct, person-by-person discovery: personally onboard likely builders/writers/learners/students, observe repeated use, record exact language and current behavior, then ask for introductions after a real result [Task 1]
  3226	- the user wants Mom Test-style conversations and two poster designs, not hypothetical “would you use this?” questions; product walkthrough videos should show real jobs and support onboarding as well as marketing [Task 1]
  3227	- payment is the shared launch gateway: web first, desktop first-class where practical, mobile deferred until production-ready; NotOrganic Provider must own browser authentication, checkout, webhooks, subscriptions, and entitlements [Task 2]
  3228	- the user wants exact status distinctions between local implementation, targeted verification, deployment, and real provider proof [Task 2]
  3229	- “remove em dashes” and use exactly four central questions when translating hiring claims into observable engineering work and evidence [Task 3]
  3230	
  3231	## Reusable knowledge
  3232	
  3233	- Stage attributable experiments: at $8 CPM, 1% CTR, and 2% visitor-to-paid conversion, $100 is a smoke test, $500 is directional, and $2,000 is larger but still noisy.   3234	- Campus/outdoor placement is permission-controlled. uOttawa external posting needs approval, bilingual French-first creative, stamped posters, and limited periods; Carleton's general policy excludes commercial promotion.   3236	- The approved hiring prompts ask about: baseline coding beyond an algorithm screen; recurring work separating junior through staff; observable evidence for solution refinement; and assessment of technical, economic, operational, and stakeholder judgment. [Task 3]

  3239

# Twyne environment variables.
# Copy to `.env.local` (gitignored) for local dev, or set these in your
# Railway service for production. `VITE_*` / `PUBLIC_*` values are inlined
# into the client bundle at BUILD time, so they must be present when the
# build command runs (not just at runtime).

# --- Convex backend (required) ---
# Convex deployment the client talks to. `root.tsx` reads PUBLIC_CONVEX_URL
# first, then falls back to VITE_CONVEX_URL.
VITE_CONVEX_URL=https://your-deployment.convex.cloud
# Convex HTTP actions / site URL (used by auth + published routes).
VITE_CONVEX_SITE_URL=https://your-deployment.convex.site
# Optional alias honored by root.tsx in addition to VITE_CONVEX_URL.
# PUBLIC_CONVEX_URL=https://your-deployment.convex.cloud
# Used by the `npx convex` CLI to target a deployment (dev/codegen only).
CONVEX_DEPLOYMENT=dev:your-deployment
# Production deploy key (Convex dashboard → Settings → Deploy keys). Set this in
# Railway: the build runs `npx convex deploy` with it to push the backend on
# every deploy. If unset, the build ships the frontend only.
# CONVEX_DEPLOY_KEY=prod:your-deployment|xxxxxxxx

# --- Auth (Better Auth) ---
# 32+ char random secret. Generate: `openssl rand -base64 32`
BETTER_AUTH_SECRET=replace-me
# Public origin of the deployed app (used for auth callbacks / cookies).
BETTER_AUTH_URL=https://www.twyne.love
# Canonical site origin (OG/canonical/ATProto redirects).
SITE_URL=https://www.twyne.love

# --- Email (Resend) ---
# Optional: Resend API key for operational email (e.g. account notices).
# RESEND_API_KEY=re_xxx
# RESEND_FROM_EMAIL=Twyne <support@twyne.love>

# --- AI providers ---
# Twyne is BYOK: end users paste their own API keys in Settings, stored
# locally in the browser. These server-side keys are optional and only
# needed if you wire a server-side provider.
# ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=
# OPENAI_API_KEY=

# --- Voice narration ---
# Optional: Pro-tier hosted voice uses OpenAI speech generation server-side.
# If unset, hosted voice falls back to OPENAI_API_KEY. BYOK voice uses the
# writer's browser-stored provider key and does not need these server vars.
# VOICE_OPENAI_API_KEY=
# VOICE_OPENAI_MODEL=gpt-4o-mini-tts
# VOICE_OPENAI_VOICE=alloy

# --- Portkey (hosted LLM gateway) — https://app.portkey.ai ---
# Optional: route all server-side AI calls through Portkey. When
# PORTKEY_API_KEY is set, Portkey takes priority over Anthropic / OpenAI /
# Rivet in the provider chain. The neuralwatt key is stored in Portkey's
# Model Catalog as provider "@neuralwatt"; model ids use the @provider/model
# form so no separate provider header is needed.
PORTKEY_API_KEY=pk-xxx
# PORTKEY_BASE_URL=https://api.portkey.ai/v1
# PORTKEY_DEFAULT_MODEL=@neuralwatt/qwen3.5-397b-fast

# --- Arize (LLM observability + evals) ---
# OpenInference tracing for every server-side generateText call in
# convex/agents.ts, plus a destination for offline experiment scoring.
# Set ARIZE_API_KEY + ARIZE_SPACE_ID in the Convex deployment env (skate
# has the values); without them the tracer stays dormant and flushArize()
# is a no-op. ARIZE_PROJECT_NAME is the Arize project the spans land in
# and matches the model_id resource attribute (default: twyne).
# ARIZE_API_KEY=
# ARIZE_SPACE_ID=
# ARIZE_PROJECT_NAME=twyne
# Arize is region-sharded; spans must go to the space's region or they 401.
# ARIZE_REGION=ca-central-1a            # us-east-1b | us-central-1a | eu-west-1a | ca-central-1a
# ARIZE_OTLP_ENDPOINT=                  # optional full override of the OTLP URL
# Keep content redacted by default. Enable only for an approved, short-lived
# production sample after confirming Arize retention and reviewer access.
# ARIZE_CAPTURE_CONTENT=false

# build command runs (not just at runtime).

# --- Convex backend (required) ---
# Convex deployment the client talks to. `root.tsx` reads PUBLIC_CONVEX_URL
# first, then falls back to VITE_CONVEX_URL.

# Convex HTTP actions / site URL (used by auth + published routes).
VITE_CONVEX_SITE_URL=https://your-deployment.convex.site
# Optional alias honored by root.tsx in addition to VITE_CONVEX_URL.
# PUBLIC_CONVEX_URL=https://your-deployment.convex.cloud
# Used by the `npx convex` CLI to target a deployment (dev/codegen only).
CONVEX_DEPLOYMENT=dev:your-deployment

# Railway: the build runs `npx convex deploy` with it to push the backend on
# every deploy. If unset, the build ships the frontend only.
# CONVEX_DEPLOY_KEY=prod:your-deployment|xxxxxxxx

# --- Auth (Better Auth) ---
# 32+ char random secret. Generate: `openssl rand -base64 32`
BETTER_AUTH_SECRET=replace-me
# Public origin of the deployed app (used for auth callbacks / cookies).
BETTER_AUTH_URL=https://www.twyne.love
# Canonical site origin (OG/canonical/ATProto redirects).
SITE_URL=https://www.twyne.love

# --- Email (Resend) ---
# Optional: Resend API key for operational email (e.g. account notices).

# RESEND_FROM_EMAIL=Twyne <support@twyne.love>

# --- AI providers ---
# Twyne is BYOK: end users paste their own API keys in Settings, stored
# locally in the browser. These server-side keys are optional and only
# needed if you wire a server-side provider.
# ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=
# OPENAI_API_KEY=

# --- Voice narration ---
# Optional: Pro-tier hosted voice uses OpenAI speech generation server-side.
# If unset, hosted voice falls back to OPENAI_API_KEY. BYOK voice uses the
# writer's browser-stored provider key and does not need these server vars.

# VOICE_OPENAI_MODEL=gpt-4o-mini-tts

# --- Portkey (hosted LLM gateway) — https://app.portkey.ai ---
# Optional: route all server-side AI calls through Portkey. When
# PORTKEY_API_KEY is set, Portkey takes priority over Anthropic / OpenAI /
# Rivet in the provider chain. The neuralwatt key is stored in Portkey's
# Model Catalog as provider "@neuralwatt"; model ids use the @provider/model
# form so no separate provider header is needed.

# PORTKEY_BASE_URL=https://api.portkey.ai/v1
# PORTKEY_DEFAULT_MODEL=@neuralwatt/qwen3.5-397b-fast

# --- Arize (LLM observability + evals) ---
# OpenInference tracing for every server-side generateText call in
# convex/agents.ts, plus a destination for offline experiment scoring.
# Set ARIZE_API_KEY + ARIZE_SPACE_ID in the Convex deployment env (skate
# has the values); without them the tracer stays dormant and flushArize()
# is a no-op. ARIZE_PROJECT_NAME is the Arize project the spans land in
# and matches the model_id resource attribute (default: twyne).
# ARIZE_API_KEY=
# ARIZE_SPACE_ID=
# ARIZE_PROJECT_NAME=twyne
# Arize is region-sharded; spans must go to the space's region or they 401.
# ARIZE_REGION=ca-central-1a            # us-east-1b | us-central-1a | eu-west-1a | ca-central-1a
# ARIZE_OTLP_ENDPOINT=                  # optional full override of the OTLP URL
# Keep content redacted by default. Enable only for an approved, short-lived
# production sample after confirming Arize retention and reviewer access.
# ARIZE_CAPTURE_CONTENT=false

content.text:
Implemented locally using Not Organic’s existing `/v1/live/sessions` route.

- Character comments now select their matching narration voice.
- Added a voice desk with duplex audio, captions, mute, and spoken editing/search actions.
- Edits support review, spoken approval, and undo.
- Added Pro gating, credit limits, and eligible first-time members’ $2.50 welcome credit.

Live currently uses Marin with the selected character’s editorial perspective.

64 focused tests passed, along with typechecks, lint, and client/server builds. **Not deployed; real microphone use and credit charging remain unverified.**

[Implementation details](/home/diogenes/Projects/twyne/docs/live-voice.md)
